name: Shoulder-width training (lateral raises, delts)

lead: Shoulder-width training grows the deltoid muscles, especially the side (lateral) heads, so the shoulders look broader. Wider-looking shoulders improve upper-body proportions and feed the broad, V-shaped frame many people aim for.

The deltoid has three heads running from the clavicle and shoulder blade to the upper arm, and the middle fibers are best placed to lift the arm out to the side, which is what a lateral raise trains. Growing that muscle adds soft-tissue thickness at the sides of the shoulder, increasing measured and apparent width; the bone underneath stays as it is. Forum members post bideltoid measurements and compare them with height. No studies test shoulder-width training as an appearance intervention, though a small body of research looks at male shoulder dimensions and perceived attractiveness in general.

paras: The usual tool is the lateral raise, trained alongside presses and rows within a regular split, often several times a week. Visible change comes over months of consistent training and is easier to see at lower body fat.

Lifting carries ordinary training risks such as shoulder strain, and forum users joke about rotator cuff damage from very high volume. Muscle adds visible width but does not change skeletal shoulder width.

angle.text: Users train the side delts, mostly with lateral raises, to make the shoulders look wider and the frame more V-shaped. Bigger lateral deltoids add soft-tissue width at the top of the torso. Forum members post bideltoid measurements against height, and muscle changes visible width but not bone width.

lead: Shoulder-width training is a looksmaxxing practice in which people train the deltoid muscles, most often with lateral raises, to make the shoulders appear wider. It is discussed in the looksmax.org community as part of improving frame and proportions, and members regularly post their "bideltoid" measurements and ask how they compare with the general population at a given height [1][2].

Anatomically, the deltoid has anterior, intermediate (lateral) and posterior heads, and the intermediate fibers are the best positioned to abduct the arm, which is the movement a lateral raise trains [3]. Proponents say that developing this muscle adds visible breadth at the top of the torso.

No clinical studies of shoulder-width training as an appearance intervention were found. A small body of attractiveness research examines male shoulder dimensions and perceived attractiveness in general, but it does not test training programs [4].

paras: The deltoid forms the rounded contour of the shoulder and arises from the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula, inserting on the humerus. When all of its fibers contract together it is the main mover for raising the arm out to the side [3].

In forum usage, "shoulder width" can mean two different things: the bone-based biacromial or clavicle width, and the soft-tissue bideltoid width measured across the outer edges of the deltoids. Training is said to affect the second but not the first. The skeletal side is covered in the article on biacromial and clavicle width.

Threads on looksmax.org include measurement comparisons, for example a user who measured about 20 to 20.5 inches across the shoulders at 6 feet 2 inches and asked whether that was average, with replies giving similar or smaller figures [1]. Posters also describe high-volume lateral raise routines as the reason their shoulders look broad, while others reply with jokes about overload sets and rotator cuff injury [2].

Members commonly pair delt training with the idea of a V-taper, in which wide shoulders contrast with a narrower waist. Proponents say clothing and posture can also change how wide the shoulders look.

Muscle growth in the deltoid adds thickness to the sides of the shoulder, so bideltoid measurements can increase with training. Wikipedia's anatomy overview describes the lateral raise as a basic abduction movement for this muscle [3]. No trial or study found here measures how much bideltoid width changes in trained appearance-focused lifters, or how observers rate the result.

No studies found. Separate research on the general topic of male body shape and attractiveness has linked shoulder measurements to perceived judgments in small samples, but it did not test training [4].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, shoulder width is treated as a key frame metric, and lateral raises are the standard answer to the question of how to widen it [1][2].

claims.claim: Lateral raises can make the shoulders visibly broader.
Bideltoid size should be compared against height to judge whether the shoulders are narrow.
Heavy or very high-volume shoulder work carries injury risk.
